title.en: Oranyan's Iron, the Cock, and the Scrap of Soil
title.zh: 奧蘭揚的鐵器、雄雞與一撮泥土

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Oduduwa's homeland, whence Oranyan set out)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：奧杜杜瓦的祖地）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale I

summary.en: When old King Oduduwa died, his youngest grandson Oranyan was away hunting and inherited only twenty-one pieces of iron, a cock, and soil tied in a rag. Spreading these on a world covered with water, he watched the cock scratch the soil across the flood until islands and dry land appeared, and the iron became the minerals under the ground.
summary.zh: 老王奧杜杜瓦去世時，最幼的孫兒奧蘭揚遠行狩獵，只分得二十一塊鐵器、一隻雄雞和一束以布包裹的泥土。他將這些攤在覆水的大地上，雄雞以爪抓散泥土，島嶼與陸地逐一浮現，鐵器則化為地下的礦藏。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition. This is the folk version of the Oduduwa-Oranyan cosmogony; told as an archival record, not as an authoritative statement for Orisha worshippers. The earth-over-water creation is a flood/first-earth motif (Thompson A812).

passages.text: The ancient King Oduduwa had a great many grandchildren, and on his death he divided among them all his possessions. But his youngest grandson, Oranyan, was at that time away hunting, and when he returned home he learnt that his brothers and cousins had inherited the old King's money, cattle, beads, and native cloths, and had left him but twenty-one pieces of iron, a cock, and some soil tied up in a rag. At that time the whole earth was covered with water, on the surface of which the people lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale I (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: The resourceful Oranyan spread upon the water his pieces of iron, and upon the iron he placed the scrap of cloth, and upon the cloth the soil, and on the soil the cock. The cock scratched with his feet and scattered the soil far and wide, so that the ocean was partly filled up and islands appeared everywhere. The pieces of iron became the mineral wealth hidden under the ground. Oranyan's brothers and cousins all desired to live on the land, and he allowed them to do so on payment of tribute; thus he became King of all the Yorubas, rich and prosperous through his grandfather's inheritance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale I (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: How Tribal Marks Came to Be Used

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Sango's royal court)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：尚戈王的宮廷）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale II

summary.en: King Sango punished a failed mission by ordering a slave cut with 122 razor marks; the healed scars so impressed the king's wives that Sango made cutting a mark of royalty instead of punishment. He could bear only two cuts, and those two cuts on the arm remain the sign of royalty.
summary.zh: 尚戈王以一百二十二道剃刀紋懲罰一位辦事不力的奴隸；傷痕癒合後竟令王妃傾慕，尚戈遂將刀紋由懲罰改為王室的標記。他自己只能忍受兩刀，自那日起臂上兩刀便成王族之記。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; etiological tale for facial/body scarification. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain King named Sango sent two slaves to a distant country on an important mission. In due course they returned, and he found that one slave had achieved successfully what he had been sent to do, while the other had accomplished nothing. The King therefore rewarded the first with high honours, and commanded the second to receive a hundred and twenty-two razor cuts all over his body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale II (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: This was a severe punishment, but when the scars healed, they gave to the slave a very remarkable appearance, which greatly took the fancy of the King's wives. Sango therefore decided that cuts should in future be given, not as punishment, but as a sign of royalty, and he placed himself at once in the hands of the markers. However, he could only bear two cuts, and so from that day two cuts on the arm have been the sign of royalty, and various other cuts came to be the marks of different tribes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale II (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Akiti the Hunter and the Elephant

region.en: Yoruba forest country (symbolic pin: forest edge near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林地帶（象徵定位：伊費城近郊林緣）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale III

summary.en: Akiti, who has beaten giant, leopard, lion, wolf and boa, calls himself King of the forest until the wise Elephant — protected by charms — challenges his claim. Spears, arrows and knives glance off; only when Akiti transforms himself into a fly, enters the Elephant's ear, and cuts its heart does he truly become the forest's king.
summary.zh: 獵人阿基提戰勝巨人、豹、獅、狼與蟒，自封「森林之王」，直到通曉符咒的大象前來挑戰。矛、箭、刀皆無法傷其身；阿基提只能化身蒼蠅，鑽入象耳直抵心臟，化回人形以獵刀剖其心，方才真正稱王。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; hero contest with charm-magic. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A famous hunter and wrestler named Akiti boasted that he was stronger than any other man or animal. He had easily overcome a giant, a leopard, a lion, a wolf, and a boa-constrictor, and as nobody else opposed his claim, he called himself the King of the forest. But he had forgotten the Elephant, who is a very wise animal and knows many charms. One day the Elephant challenged him, declaring that he had no right to call himself King, as the Elephant himself was the monarch of the forest and could not be defeated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale III (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Akiti flung his spear, but because of the Elephant's charm the weapon glanced off his hide and did him no harm; bow, poisoned arrows, and hunting-knife availed nothing. The hunter then used his own charm and changed himself into a lion and flew at the Elephant, but was flung off; next he became a serpent, but could not crush the Elephant to death. At last he changed himself into a fly, flew into the Elephant's large flapping ear, went right down inside until he came to the heart, changed into a man again, and cut up the heart with his hunting-knife. The Elephant fell dead, and Akiti stepped out of his body in triumph, now without question the King of the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale III (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: royal court at Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：奧約王廷）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale IV

summary.en: A young prince complains that his allotted territory is too small and its people too few; his father, displeased, turns a great bundle of sticks into human beings and gives them to him as subjects. The tribe thenceforth bears the nickname Omo Igi, Sons of Sticks.
summary.zh: 一位年輕王子抱怨父親分給他的封地太小、子民太少；國王不悅，便將一大捆木棍化為人形，賜給兒子作臣民。該族自此得名「奧莫伊吉」——木棍之子。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition. Tagged clay-humans as the nearest motif (humans manufactured from base matter); the material is wood, not clay — an interpretive substitution. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A great King sent his various sons to rule over different parts of his kingdom, and all were satisfied but one, the youngest and most ambitious, who returned to his father after some time with the complaint that his territory was much too small and his subjects too few. The King was displeased with his son, and sent for a large bundle of sticks, which he converted into human beings. "Here are some more subjects for you!" he said to the astonished Prince. From that time the tribe was famous for its strength and stupidity, and went by the nickname of Sons of Sticks, or Omo Igi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale IV (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: village path near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊村徑）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale V

summary.en: A quarrelling woman digs a pit on the path to the well; when her rival falls in and is hauled out by the hair, the hair stretches long — a shameful oddity that becomes a coveted beauty, until every woman jumps into the pit to be pulled out by her hair.
summary.zh: 兩名婦人爭吵，其一在井邊路上掘深坑；宿敵墜坑後被眾人抓髮拉起，頭髮愈拉愈長。起初羞愧難當，後竟成艷羨之美，眾婦爭相跳坑任人拉髮，女子長髮自此而來。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; etiological folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Two women quarrelled, and one of them went out secretly at night and dug a deep pit in the middle of the path leading from her enemy's house to the village well. Early next morning, when all were going to the well for water with jars balanced on their heads, this woman fell into the pit and cried loudly for help. Her friends ran to her and, seizing her by the hair, began to pull her out; to their surprise, her hair stretched as they pulled, and by the time she was safely on the path, her hair was as long as a man's arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale V (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: At first she hid herself in shame, but soon she saw that her long hair was beautiful and scorned the short-haired women. They, consumed with jealousy, began to be ashamed of their own hair. "We have men's hair. How beautiful it would be to have long hair!" So one by one they jumped into the pit, and their friends pulled them out by the hair — and in this way they, and all women after them, had long hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale V (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Sango Calls Down Lightning on His Own Palace

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: palace below the hill)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：山腳王宮）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale VI

summary.en: Sango tries a lightning-attracting charm on his own palace, which burns with his whole family inside; in grief and rage he executes 160 courtiers, abandons his rule, and takes his own life when deserted. His people bury him honourably and worship him as god of thunder — and to this day Yorubas cry "Long live the King!" when thunder follows lightning.
summary.zh: 尚戈在自宮試驗引雷之咒，宮殿焚毀闔家罹難；他悲怒交加處死一百六十名近臣，棄國出走，眾叛親離後自盡。族人厚葬之，奉為雷神。至今約魯巴人見雷隨電至，必呼「國王萬歲！」。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the death-and-deification of Sango, the thunder orisha and third king of Oyo. Sensitively embedded in ongoing Shango devotion. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: King Sango was acquainted with many deadly charms, and he once happened to discover a preparation by which he could attract lightning. He foolishly decided to try the effect of the charm first of all on his own palace, which was at the foot of a hill. Ascending the hill with his courtiers, the King employed the charm; a storm suddenly arose, the palace was struck by lightning and burnt to the ground, together with Sango's whole family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VI (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Overcome with grief at the loss of his possessions and above all his sons, the impetuous King resolved to rule no more. In his rage he executed a hundred and sixty of his courtiers — eighty who had disagreed with his plan, and eighty who had agreed too eagerly. Then, accompanied by a few friends, he left the place; one by one they deserted him, and in despair he put an end to his own life. His people came to the spot and gave him an honourable funeral, and he was ever afterwards worshipped as the god of thunder and lightning. So, when the Yorubas see the flash of lightning followed by the sullen roar of thunder, they remember Sango's rage and exclaim: "Long live the King!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VI (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba river country (symbolic pin: riverside near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴河鄉（象徵定位：奧約近郊河畔）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale VII

summary.en: Imprisoned in a sealed hut to starve, an Olofin spares the mouse he was about to eat; the grateful mouse returns with a troop of mice bearing grain and fruit that keep the king alive for five days. His captors, convinced he must be a powerful charmer, free him and send him home in a war-canoe.
summary.zh: 奧洛芬王被囚於無門無窗的茅屋中等死，他舉刀欲食一鼠，旋即心生憐憫放下刀。知恩的鼠群連日送來穀物乾糧，五日後仇家開屋，見王安好如常，深信他有強大符咒，遂釋之，並以戰舟送其歸國。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; mercy-to-animals folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A famous Olofin, or Yoruba King, was once imprisoned by his enemies in a hut without any door or roof-opening, and left to die of starvation. As he sat gloomily on the ground, he saw a little mouse running across the hut and seized his knife, exclaiming: "Rather than die of hunger, I will eat this mouse!" But on second thoughts he put away his knife, saying: "Why should I kill the mouse? I shall starve later on, just the same."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: To his surprise the mouse addressed him: "Noble King! Greetings to you on your generosity! You have spared my life, and in return I will spare yours." The mouse disappeared into a hole and returned followed by twenty or thirty other mice, all bearing grains of corn, gari, and small fruits. For five days they fed him in this manner, and on the sixth day the captors opened the hut, astonished to find him alive and in good health. "This Olofin must have a powerful charm!" they declared. "It appears that he can live without eating or drinking!" Thereupon they released him, gave him a war-canoe, and let him return in freedom to his own country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Iroko Tree and Its Wandering Spirit

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: grove near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊樹叢）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale VIII

summary.en: In the great iroko tree lives an old man's spirit that prowls at night with a little torch; meeting it face to face brings madness and death, and cutting iroko wood brings misfortune on woodcutter and family. Even furniture of iroko groans at night — the imprisoned spirit longing for the forest.
summary.zh: 巨大的伊羅科樹中棲著一位老人的魂魄，夜裡提著小火把遊蕩，直視其面者瘋癲而亡；砍伐伊羅科木者全家招殃。凡以此木製傢俱之屋，夜半常聞呻吟吱呀之聲——那是被囚的樹靈，渴望重歸林間。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the iroko remains a feared and ritually significant tree. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: In the forest there is a giant tree called by the Yorubas the Iroko, which is shunned by all people, for in it lives the spirit of an old man who prowls about at night with a little torch and frightens travellers. Anyone who sees the Iroko-man face to face goes mad and speedily dies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VIII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeing the thick branches and mighty trunk of the Iroko, woodcutters are often tempted to cut the tree down, but this is very unlucky, as it brings the displeasure of the Iroko-man and misfortune on the woodcutter and all his family. In any house which contains furniture made of Iroko-wood, strange groaning and creaking noises are heard at night: it is the spirit of the Iroko, imprisoned in the wood, who longs to wander about again through the forest with his little torch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale VIII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Orisa Oko and the Demon Polo
title.zh: 奧里莎奧科與惡魔波洛

region.en: Yoruba farmland (symbolic pin: cave country near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴農鄉（象徵定位：伊費附近岩洞地帶）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale IX

summary.en: A solitary old hunter with a fife and dog becomes a renowned soothsayer in a cave, where suspected witches are led and beheaded by the demon Polo he keeps. After his death, his followers hide a strongman as the "demon" — until a muscular accused kills the impostor, the fraud is exposed, and the cave is abandoned forever.
summary.zh: 一位孑然一身的獵人以笛聲喚犬引路，老來棲身岩洞，成了聲名遠播的占者。凡涉嫌巫術者被拖至洞前，無辜者由他親手引出，有罪者則由他所豢養的惡魔「波洛」斬首擲出。老人死後，信徒藏一壯漢假扮惡魔，直到某日一名魁梧嫌犯反將假惡魔殺死、毫髮無傷走出洞穴，騙局敗露，聖洞自此荒廢。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; orisha Oko is the agriculture deity — here the tale treats his cave-oracle cult satirically. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Orisa Oko was a poor hunter, solitary save for his fife and his dog. If ever he lost his way in the fields or the forest, he would play a plaintive melody on his fife, and the sounds would lead the faithful dog to his side to guide him home. As years went by he grew too old for hunting and took up residence in a cave; people thought him more mysterious than ever, came to him for advice about the future, and he won great renown as a soothsayer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale IX (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: In those days witchcraft was punished by death, and anyone suspected of the evil art was dragged to Orisa Oko's cave. If the soothsayer found him innocent, he led him forth by the hand; if guilty, his head was cut off and thrown to the waiting crowd by the demon Polo, which Orisa Oko kept in the cave. After the old hunter's death his followers hid a very strong man in the cave to act as the demon. But one day a tall, muscular man was accused, and it was the head of the supposed "demon" that came rolling out instead — soon the strong man reappeared unharmed and triumphant. The people, indignant at the deception, deserted the cave of Orisa Oko from that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale IX (1929); not verbatim.

title.zh: 莫雷米與草甲伊格博人

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Moremi's city and the stream of her vow)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：莫雷米之城與許願之溪）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale X

summary.en: The Ife noblewoman Moremi lets herself be captured by the terrifying Igbos, learns they are ordinary men in mantles of dry grass who fear fire, and escapes to tell her people. The Ifes defeat them with torches; but the stream-god she had promised a sacrifice demands her son Ela, who — only half dead on the altar — climbs a rope of grass to heaven, to return one day and reap his mother's sacrifice.
summary.zh: 伊費貴婦莫雷米自願落入可怕的伊格博人手中，探得他們不過是身披乾草戰甲、畏懼火焰的凡人，逃歸後獻計火攻，敵人大敗。然而她曾向溪神許下重願，神竟索其子埃拉為祭。埃拉臥於祭壇僅半死，甦醒後以草繩攀上天界，終有一日將歸來領受母親犧牲之果。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Moremi is one of Ile-Ife's most honoured heroines with an active cult and festival (Edi). Presented as an archival folktale record.

passages.text: A nobleman of Ile-Ife had a beautiful and virtuous wife named Moremi, and a handsome young son, Ela. The country of the Ifes was subject to fierce raids by a tribe called the Igbos, whose uncanny appearance in battle made the Ifes think them not human but a visitation sent by the gods in punishment for some evil. In vain did they offer sacrifices; the raids continued and the land was thrown into panic. The heroic Moremi resolved to let herself be captured during a raid, so that she might be carried to the land of the Igbos and learn their secrets. Bidding farewell to her husband and little son, she went to a certain stream and promised its god that, if her attempt succeeded, she would offer him the richest sacrifice she could afford.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale X (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Captured as she planned, she was given as a slave to the King of the Igbos and soon rose to a position of importance, learning that the raiders were not gods but ordinary men who wore strange mantles of grass and bamboo fibre and were much afraid of fire. She escaped home; her tidings were joyfully received at Ile-Ife, and the Igbos were utterly defeated by the trick she had suggested. But when Moremi made her great sacrifice of sheep, fowls, and bullocks, the god of the stream demanded the life of her son. Sorrowing, she consented and sacrificed the boy Ela — yet he was only half dead; when the people had departed he recovered, sprang up, made a rope of grass, climbed up to heaven, and it is certain that he will one day return to reap the benefits of his mother's noble sacrifice. The Ifes wept at the spectacle and promised to be her sons and daughters for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale X (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Bat Hides by Day

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: rafters near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊屋簷）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XI

summary.en: Half bird and half rodent, the Bat fights among the rats until the birds seem likely to win, then flies up to change sides. Both disgusted hosts turn on him together, and ever since he hides in dark places by day and ventures out only in the evening.
summary.zh: 蝙蝠半鳥半鼠，原與鼠親並肩作戰，見鳥將勝便飛上半空倒戈。兩軍皆惡其背信，罷戰合攻蝙蝠。自那日起，牠白天躲藏於暗處，唯有暮色降臨方敢露面。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal folktale of treachery punished. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: The Bat is half a bird and half a rodent, and lives partly on the earth and partly in the air, but both rats and birds shun him, and this is why: the rats, his cousins, were once fighting a great battle with the birds, and Bat fought in their midst. But when he saw that the birds were likely to be victorious, he left the rats and flew up into the air to fight on the side of the birds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XI (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Both the rats and the birds were disgusted at this cowardly action, so they ceased from fighting one another and all combined to attack the Bat. Since that day he has been forced to hide in dark places all day, and only comes out in the evening when his enemies cannot see him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XI (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Leopard-Man and the Forest Bride

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: river woods near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊河林）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XII

summary.en: A silent, handsome stranger comes monthly to a village; a maiden follows him into the forest against repeated warnings. At a leopard-skin under a tree he sings that he is in truth a savage leopard, resumes that form, and pursues her. A tree falls across a river to save her, she reaches the village, and the leopard-man is never seen again.
summary.zh: 一位沉默俊美的陌生人每月造訪村中，少女不聽再三勸阻執意隨他入林。在樹下的豹皮旁，他歌道自己實為兇豹，隨即現出原形追逐少女。危急之際一棵樹倒臥河上助她渡河，她終於逃回村中，豹郎從此絕跡。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; were-animal marriage tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A handsome Stranger once came into a certain village and strolled about among the people in mysterious silence. All the maidens admired him and wished that he would choose one of them for his bride; but he said nothing and at last walked away into the forest. A month later he came again, and this time one of the maidens fell so much in love with him that she resolved to follow him, for she could not bear to be separated from him. He stopped and begged her to return home; but she would not: "I will never leave you, and wherever you go, I will follow." "Beautiful maiden, you will regret it," replied the stranger sadly — and said so again at his second stop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Deep in the forest they reached a tree at the foot of which lay a leopard-skin. Standing under it, the stranger sang a melancholy song telling her that though he was allowed once a month to wander like a man, he was in reality a savage leopard and would rend her in pieces as soon as he regained his natural form. He flung himself on the ground, became a snarling leopard, and pursued her. Fear gave speed to her feet; as he pursued, he sang that he would tear her in small pieces, and she replied in song that he would never overtake her. At a deep but narrow river a tree took pity on her and fell across it so she could cross. Nearly exhausted, she reached the village in safety; the leopard slunk back into the forest, and the handsome stranger was never seen again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Water-Bird Stands on One Leg

region.en: Yoruba lagoon country (symbolic pin: coastal lagoon near Lagos)
region.zh: 約魯巴潟湖之鄉（象徵定位：拉哥斯近郊湖畔）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XIII

summary.en: A water-bird swallows the King of the crabs; the crab tribe vows to nip off the bird's bright pink legs in revenge. The water-rat warns the bird and advises a disguise: standing on one leg. The crabs, seeing a one-legged pink creature, pass by — and the bird stands on one leg to this day.
summary.zh: 一隻涉禽吞下了蟹王，蟹族憤而立誓報復，要夾斷牠那雙粉紅亮腿。水鼠聞訊報信，教牠收起一足裝作異鳥。蟹群見了獨腿高鳥，道「我們的仇敵有兩腿，此必非牠」，逕自離去。涉禽自此單足獨立至今。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A water-bird once, in search of food, swallowed the King of the crabs, and the whole tribe of crabs were so enraged that they swore they would have their revenge. "We will find this horrible bird and nip off its legs. We shall not fail to find it, for its legs are bright pink in colour and its feathers are pink and white."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the water-rat overheard the crabs plotting and hastened to tell the water-bird. "They will nip off my beautiful pink legs, and then what will become of me?" cried the bird. "It is very simple," replied the water-rat: "if you stand on one leg, they will think you are some other creature." The bird tucked up one leg; when the crabs came they saw, as they thought, a very tall pink bird with one leg and a large beak. "Our enemy has two legs. This cannot be he." And they passed by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ants and the Miser's Treasure

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊院落）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XIV

summary.en: A poor man feeds ants and parrots; a cruel miser hoards gold and crushes their kindred. The ants dig a tunnel from the miser's hut to the poor man's house and carry the treasure over three nights — but when the tunnel's end is found, the poor man is condemned as a witch, until the ants devour his hut overnight so the villagers believe the gods have punished him in their stead.
summary.zh: 窮漢以碎穀飼蟻餵鳥；吝嗇鬼囤金虐生。蟻群掘地道，三夜之間將守財奴的金子搬入窮漢屋中。地道被發現後，窮漢被誣為施法竊金、翌日將焚身。蟻群連夜噬毀囚屋，村人誤以為天罰已代行其刑，蟻群卻獨知真相。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal-justice folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There once was a poor man who was very kind to animals and birds; however little he had, he always spared a few grains for his parrot and spread titbits every morning for the industrious ants. In the same village lived a miser who had by crafty means collected a large store of gold, which he kept tied up in the corner of a hut, sitting outside all day and night. He threw stones at any bird and crushed any ant he found, for he detested every living creature and loved nothing but his gold. When he had killed a great many of their number, the ants began to think how they might punish his cruelty. "What a pity it is," said the King of the ants, "that our friend is a poor man, while our enemy is so rich!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIV (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the ants dug a great tunnel, one end in the poor man's house and the other in the miser's hut, and over three nights carried the whole treasure into the poor man's house, who rejoiced, thinking the gods had rewarded his years of humble toil. The miser accused witchcraft; the tunnel was traced, the gold found under native cloths in the poor man's hut, and he was shut up to be burnt alive. The ants, sorely perplexed at what their plan had wrought, ate up the whole of the prison-hut overnight. In the morning the people said: "The gods have taken the punishment out of our hands! The ants have devoured both the hut and the prisoner!" And only the ants knew that this was not true.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIV (1929); not verbatim.
